lessons.title: Variables
lessons.summary:
Variables store information your program can use later. Think of them like labeled boxes — you give the box a name and put something inside.

There are three ways to create variables:
- `const` — the value never changes (use this by default)
- `let` — the value can change
- `var` — old way, avoid it

When to use what:
Use `const` for everything by default. Switch to `let` only when you know the value will change, like a counter or a loop variable.
lessons.example:
const name = "Daniel"   // never changes
let score = 0           // can change
score = 10              // allowed with let

const age = 20
// age = 21  // ERROR — const cannot be reassigned

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary:
Functions are reusable blocks of code. Instead of writing the same code over and over, you write it once inside a function and call it whenever you need it.

Think of a function like a recipe — you write the steps once, then follow the recipe whenever you want to cook that dish.

Key concepts:
- Parameters are the inputs a function accepts
- Return sends a value back to whoever called the function
- Arrow functions are the modern preferred way to write functions

lessons.title: Array Methods (map, filter, reduce)
lessons.summary:
Array methods let you work with lists of data in a clean and powerful way. The three most important ones are map, filter, and reduce.

Think of arrays like a list of items, and these methods as tools to work with that list.

lessons.title: Async/Await
lessons.summary:
JavaScript is single-threaded — it does one thing at a time. But some things take time, like fetching data from an API. Async/await lets you wait for those things without freezing the whole program.

Think of it like ordering food at a restaurant. You place the order (start the request), do other things while waiting, and when it arrives (data comes back) you eat (use the data).

Key concepts:
- `async` makes a function asynchronous
- `await` pauses until the promise resolves
- Always wrap in try/catch to handle errors

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.summary: Objects store related data together using key-value pairs. Think of an object like a profile card — it holds multiple pieces of information about one thing.

lessons.title: Destructuring
lessons.summary:
Destructuring lets you pull values out of arrays and objects quickly, without writing multiple lines of code.

Think of it like unpacking a suitcase — instead of taking out each item one by one, you unpack everything at once.

lessons.title: Template Literals
lessons.summary: Template literals let you embed variables directly inside strings. Instead of using + to combine strings, you use backticks and ${} to insert values cleanly.
lessons.example:
const name = "Daniel"
const age = 20

// Old way (messy)
"Hello, " + name + "! You are " + age + " years old."

// Template literal (clean)
`Hello, ${name}! You are ${age} years old.`

// Multi-line strings
const message = `
  Welcome back, ${name}.
  Your account is active.
`

lessons.title: Error Handling (try/catch)
lessons.summary:
Things go wrong in code — APIs fail, data is missing, users enter bad input. Error handling lets you catch those problems and respond gracefully instead of crashing.

Key concepts:
- `try` — run the risky code
- `catch` — handle the error if something goes wrong
- `finally` — always runs, whether success or failure

lessons.title: Basic Types (string, number, boolean)
lessons.summary:
TypeScript adds types to JavaScript. Types tell the computer what kind of data a variable holds, catching mistakes before your code runs.

Think of types like labels on containers — "this box holds numbers" prevents you from accidentally putting text in it.

lessons.title: Interfaces
lessons.summary: Interfaces define the shape of an object — what properties it must have and what types they should be. They're like a contract your data must follow.

lessons.title: Type Aliases
lessons.summary: Type aliases create a custom name for a type. Similar to interfaces but more flexible — you can use them for primitives, unions, and more.

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.summary:
Generics let you write reusable code that works with different types. Instead of writing the same function for strings and for numbers, you write it once with a generic type.

Think of generics like a template — fill in the type when you use it.

lessons.title: Union Types
lessons.summary: Union types let a variable hold more than one type. Use the | symbol to say "this can be A or B."

lessons.title: Utility Types (Partial, Omit, Record)
lessons.summary: Utility types are built-in TypeScript helpers that transform existing types. They save you from rewriting types by hand.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
lessons.summary:
Semantic HTML uses tags that describe what they contain. Instead of using `<div>` for everything, you use meaningful tags that tell browsers and screen readers what each section is.

This improves accessibility, SEO, and makes your code easier to read.
lessons.example:
```html
...
Home About
...
...
``` **Common semantic tags:** - `header` — top of page or section - `nav` — navigation links - `main` — main content - `section` — grouped content - `article` — standalone content - `footer` — bottom of page

lessons.title: Flexbox
lessons.summary:
Flexbox makes it easy to lay out elements in a row or column. The parent becomes a flex container and controls how children are arranged.

Think of it like a shelf — you decide if items go left-to-right or top-to-bottom, how spaced out they are, and how they align.

lessons.title: CSS Grid
lessons.summary:
CSS Grid is for two-dimensional layouts — rows AND columns at the same time. Perfect for page layouts, dashboards, and card grids.

Flexbox is one direction. Grid is both directions.

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.summary: Responsive design makes your website look good on all screen sizes — phone, tablet, and desktop. You use media queries to apply different styles at different screen widths.

lessons.title: Variables and Data Types
lessons.summary: Python variables don't need a type declaration — Python figures it out automatically. This is called dynamic typing.
lessons.example:
name = "Daniel"        # string
age = 20               # integer
height = 5.11          # float
is_active = True       # boolean
skills = ["JS", "Python"]  # list
user = {"name": "Daniel"}  # dictionary

# f-strings (like template literals)
print(f"Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.")

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Functions in Python use the `def` keyword and indentation instead of curly braces.
lessons.example:
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

# With default parameter
def greet(name="stranger"):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

greet("Daniel")   # "Hello, Daniel!"
greet()           # "Hello, stranger!"

# Lambda (like arrow functions)
double = lambda x: x * 2
double(5)  # 10

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: Python loops are clean and readable. The `for` loop works great with lists and ranges.
lessons.example:
# For loop
for i in range(5):
    print(i)  # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

# Loop through a list
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

# While loop
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

# List comprehension (powerful shortcut)
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10)]

lessons.title: Conditionals
lessons.summary: Python uses `if`, `elif`, and `else`. Indentation is how Python knows what's inside each block — no curly braces needed.

lessons.title: Lists and Dictionaries
lessons.summary: Lists are ordered collections. Dictionaries store key-value pairs. These are Python's most used data structures.
lessons.example:
# List
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("mango")
fruits.remove("apple")
fruits[0]  # "banana"

# Dictionary
user = {
    "name": "Daniel",
    "age": 20,
    "skills": ["Python", "JavaScript"]
}
user["name"]          # "Daniel"
user["city"] = "Dallas"  # add new key
user.get("email", "N/A") # safe access with default

lessons.title: SELECT queries
lessons.summary: SELECT is how you read data from a database. It's the most used SQL command — you'll write it constantly.

lessons.title: JOINs
lessons.summary: JOINs combine data from multiple tables. The most common is INNER JOIN — it returns rows where there's a match in both tables.
lessons.example:
-- Tables: users and orders
-- Each order has a user_id

-- INNER JOIN — only matching rows
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM users
INNER JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;

-- LEFT JOIN — all users, even without orders
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM users
LEFT JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
lessons.summary: These are the write operations in SQL — creating, changing, and removing data.
lessons.example:
-- INSERT — add new row
INSERT INTO users (name, email, age)
VALUES ('Daniel', 'daniel@example.com', 20);

-- UPDATE — change existing row
UPDATE users
SET age = 21
WHERE id = 1;

-- DELETE — remove row
DELETE FROM users
WHERE id = 1;

-- CAREFUL — DELETE without WHERE deletes everything!

lessons.title: Components
lessons.summary:
Components are the building blocks of React. Every piece of UI is a component — a button, a card, a nav bar. They're just functions that return JSX.

Build small components and combine them into bigger ones. Like LEGO blocks.

lessons.title: useState
lessons.summary: useState lets your component remember and update data. When state changes, React automatically re-renders the component to show the new data.

lessons.title: useEffect
lessons.summary: useEffect runs code after the component renders. Use it for fetching data, setting up subscriptions, or anything that needs to happen after the UI appears.

lessons.title: File-Based Routing
lessons.summary: In Next.js you don't set up a router manually. Just create a file and it becomes a page automatically. The file name and folder structure define the URL.
lessons.example:
app/
  page.tsx              →  /
  about/
    page.tsx            →  /about
  blog/
    page.tsx            →  /blog
    [id]/
      page.tsx          →  /blog/123
  api/
    users/
      route.ts          →  /api/users

lessons.title: Server vs Client Components
lessons.summary: Next.js has two types of components. Server components run on the server and are faster — use them by default. Client components run in the browser and are needed for interactivity.

lessons.title: What is Node.js
lessons.summary: Node.js lets you run JavaScript on the server — outside of the browser. Before Node.js, JavaScript only worked in browsers. Now you can use the same language for frontend and backend.

lessons.title: HTTP Module
lessons.summary: Node.js has a built-in HTTP module for creating servers. This is what Express builds on top of.

lessons.title: Setting up a server
lessons.summary: Express makes building servers much simpler than the raw Node.js HTTP module. Less code, cleaner syntax, same result.

lessons.title: Routes (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
lessons.summary: Routes define how your server responds to different requests. Each route has a method (GET, POST, etc.) and a path.

lessons.title: Utility Classes
lessons.summary:
Tailwind CSS uses utility classes — small, single-purpose classes you combine directly in your HTML. No writing custom CSS files.

Instead of writing `.button { background: blue; padding: 8px 16px; }` you write `bg-blue-500 px-4 py-2` directly on the element.
lessons.example:
Card Title

Card description here.

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.summary: Tailwind makes responsive design easy with breakpoint prefixes. Add `md:` or `lg:` before any class to apply it only at that screen size.
lessons.example:
```html
Left
Right
Home About
``` **Breakpoints:** - `sm:` — 640px and up - `md:` — 768px and up - `lg:` — 1024px and up - `xl:` — 1280px and up

lessons.title: Git Basics (add, commit, push)
lessons.summary:
Git tracks changes to your code over time. Think of it like a save system — you can always go back to any previous version of your project.

The three commands you use every day:
lessons.example:
```bash
# Stage changes (tell Git what to include)
git add .

# Save a snapshot with a message
git commit -m "feat: add login page"

# Send to GitHub
git push origin main

# See what changed
git status

# See commit history
git log --oneline
```

**Good commit message format:**
- `feat:` — new feature
- `fix:` — bug fix
- `docs:` — documentation
- `refactor:` — code cleanup

lessons.title: Branching
lessons.summary: Branches let you work on new features without touching the main code. Create a branch, do your work, then merge it back when ready.
lessons.example:
# Create and switch to new branch
git checkout -b feature/login-page

# See all branches
git branch

# Switch between branches
git checkout main

# Merge branch into main
git merge feature/login-page

# Delete branch after merging
git branch -d feature/login-page

lessons.title: Basic Commands (pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, rm)
lessons.summary: The terminal lets you control your computer with text commands. Every developer uses it daily — running servers, installing packages, managing files.
lessons.example:
pwd              # show current directory
ls               # list files
ls -la           # list all files including hidden

cd projects      # go into folder
cd ..            # go back one level
cd ~             # go to home directory

mkdir my-app     # create folder
touch index.js   # create file
rm file.txt      # delete file
rm -rf folder/   # delete folder (careful!)

cat file.txt     # read file contents
echo "hello"     # print text

lessons.title: Grep and Find
lessons.summary: Grep searches inside files for text. Find searches for files by name. Both are powerful tools for navigating large codebases.
lessons.example:
# Search for text inside files
grep "TODO" file.js
grep -r "TODO" .           # search all files recursively
grep -r "useState" src/    # find all useState usages

# Find files by name
find . -name "*.tsx"       # all TypeScript React files
find . -name "index.js"    # find index.js anywhere
find . -type f -name "*.env" # find env files

lessons.title: Pull Requests
lessons.summary:
Pull Requests (PRs) are how you propose changes to a codebase. Instead of pushing directly to main, you push to a branch and open a PR for review.

This is how every professional team works.

**Steps:**
```bash
# 1. Create a branch
git checkout -b feature/new-button

# 2. Make changes and commit
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add new button component"

# 3. Push branch to GitHub
git push origin feature/new-button

# 4. Go to GitHub and click "Compare & pull request"
# 5. Add description and submit
# 6. After review — merge the PR
```

lessons.title: GitHub Actions (CI/CD)
lessons.summary: GitHub Actions automates tasks when you push code. The most common use is CI/CD — automatically running tests and deploying your app when you push to main.
lessons.example:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm run build

lessons.title: HTTP Methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
lessons.summary: REST APIs use HTTP methods to define what action you want to perform. Think of them like verbs — GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes.

lessons.title: Status Codes (200, 400, 401, 404, 500)
lessons.summary:
Every API response includes a status code that tells you if the request succeeded or failed.

**Common codes:**
```
200 — OK (success)
201 — Created (new resource made)
400 — Bad Request (you sent wrong data)
401 — Unauthorized (not logged in)
403 — Forbidden (logged in but no permission)
404 — Not Found (resource doesn't exist)
500 — Internal Server Error (something broke on the server)
```

lessons.title: How JWT works
lessons.summary:
JWT (JSON Web Token) is how apps handle authentication. After logging in, the server gives you a token. You send that token with every future request to prove who you are.

Think of it like a concert wristband — show your ID once at the door, get a wristband, then flash the wristband everywhere else.

**The flow:**
```
1. User logs in with email + password
2. Server verifies credentials
3. Server creates a JWT token
4. Client stores the token
5. Every request includes the token in the header
6. Server verifies the token on each request
```

lessons.title: Sliding Window
lessons.summary:
Sliding Window is a technique for working with arrays or strings. Instead of using nested loops (slow), you maintain a window that slides through the data (fast).

Use it when you need to find a subarray or substring that meets some condition.

lessons.title: Two Pointers
lessons.summary:
Two Pointers uses two variables moving through data — usually one from each end. It replaces nested loops with a single loop, making your code much faster.

Use it on sorted arrays when looking for pairs or comparing from both sides.

lessons.title: Hash Maps
lessons.summary: Hash Maps (objects in JavaScript) store key-value pairs for O(1) lookup — instant access regardless of size. Use them for counting, grouping, and caching.

lessons.title: DRY principle
lessons.summary:
DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. If you write the same code more than once, extract it into a function or component.

Repeated code means if you need to change something, you have to change it in multiple places — leading to bugs.

lessons.title: Writing a workflow file
lessons.summary: GitHub Actions workflows are written in YAML files stored in `.github/workflows/`. They define what happens when you push code, open a PR, or on a schedule.
lessons.example:
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test-and-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

lessons.title: Vercel (frontend)
lessons.summary:
Vercel is the easiest way to deploy Next.js and React apps. Connect your GitHub repo and every push to main automatically deploys your app.

**Steps:**
```
1. Go to vercel.com
2. Click "New Project"
3. Import your GitHub repo
4. Configure build settings (usually auto-detected)
5. Add environment variables
6. Click Deploy

Every push to main → auto deploys
Every PR → preview deployment
```

lessons.title: Environment variables in production
lessons.summary: Environment variables store sensitive data like API keys and database URLs outside your code. Never hardcode secrets — never commit them to GitHub.
lessons.example:
# .env file (never commit this)
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@host/db
JWT_SECRET=your-secret-key
GEMINI_API_KEY=your-api-key

# .env.example (commit this — shows what variables are needed)
DATABASE_URL=
JWT_SECRET=
GEMINI_API_KEY=
```

```js
// Access in Node.js
const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL

// Access in Next.js (must prefix with NEXT_PUBLIC_ for client)
const apiUrl = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL

lessons.title: What is PostgreSQL
lessons.summary:
PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database. Data is stored in tables with rows and columns — like a spreadsheet, but much more powerful and queryable.

You've already used it in Magnifit and FinderDallas through Supabase.

lessons.title: Relationships (one-to-many)
lessons.summary: Tables can be related to each other. A user can have many posts. A post belongs to one user. This is called a one-to-many relationship.
lessons.example:
-- Users table
CREATE TABLE users (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
);

-- Posts table (belongs to a user)
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  content TEXT,
  user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),  -- foreign key
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Get all posts with author name
SELECT posts.title, users.name AS author
FROM posts
INNER JOIN users ON posts.user_id = users.id;

lessons.title: What is NoSQL
lessons.summary:
MongoDB is a NoSQL database — instead of tables and rows, it stores documents (like JSON objects) in collections. More flexible than SQL but less structured.

When to use SQL vs NoSQL:
- SQL (PostgreSQL) → structured data, relationships, financial data
- NoSQL (MongoDB) → flexible data, rapid prototyping, content
